result:
**Meanwhile**

There is a last time you are carried to bed, and no one marks it. Some evening in your fifth or sixth year, the arms that have carried you a thousand nights carry you a thousand-and-first, and then never again, and nobody in the house knows that a thing has ended. The arms go on to other work. Dishes, probably.

I think about this more than is useful. Not to be maudlin — the maudlin version is a greeting card, and I want the other version, the one that's actually strange. What's strange is not that things end. It's that endings almost never announce themselves. We have ceremonies for beginnings: the ribbon cut, the bottle broken on the hull, the name spoken over the child. For endings we have funerals, which arrive far too late, and graduations, which are about something else. Everything in between simply stops occurring, and the stopping is invisible, and we find out years later by accident, if at all.

Consider the last time you played a game outdoors with the neighborhood kids. There was a final round of whatever it was, and one of you was called in to dinner, and you all said *tomorrow* and meant it, and tomorrow it rained, and then it was some other season and you had grown into other bodies with other appetites. No one lost that game. It's still open. Somewhere in a yard that has since been resodded, the score is 4–3 and the light is going.

Or: the last time someone alive spoke a language. There are documented cases — a woman in her eighties, the last fluent speaker, and after her the words exist only as sounds on tape, orphaned. But there was also a last conversation, before that: the last time two people used the language *to each other*, to say something ordinary. Pass the salt. It's cold out. You look tired. And they wouldn't have known. Neither one thought: this is the final time this grammar will do the work grammar is for. They just ate their dinner.

I find I don't want to draw the obvious moral. The obvious moral is *cherish every moment*, and it's not only impossible, it's a bad idea. A moment cherished is a moment held at arm's length and examined, and most of what makes a life livable requires being inside it stupidly, unreflectively, the way you're inside a warm bath or an argument. If you spent the last game of catch knowing it was the last, it would be ruined. You'd be performing. Your father would notice you'd gone weird and ask what was wrong. The unmarked quality of endings might be a mercy — or at least an efficiency, the way it's efficient that you can't feel your own heartbeat unless you go looking.

What interests me instead is the word *meanwhile*.

Meanwhile is the widest word in English. It's the one that admits everything else is still happening. While you were reading that paragraph about lost languages, someone was being told a diagnosis and someone was catching a bus with unexpected ease and a great many people were doing nothing much, which is the most common human activity by an enormous margin and the least represented in literature. There is a whole genre of thought that consists of remembering *meanwhile* — that the person who cut you off in traffic is at the center of their own novel, that the city you're bored in contains someone's best day. It's a cheap trick and it works every time, on me anyway. I use it when I'm irritated. I say the word to myself: *meanwhile*. And the frame widens, and the irritation doesn't disappear but it gets smaller relative to the field, which is all you can really ask of a feeling.

Here's what I suspect. I suspect that the unnoticed endings and the vast *meanwhile* are the same fact seen from two sides. Both are consequences of the world being much larger than attention. Attention is a narrow instrument — a flashlight in a warehouse — and the warehouse doesn't stop being full when the beam moves on. Things end outside the beam. Things begin out there too. Right now some habit is forming in you that will define a decade, and you can't see it, because habits are invisible at the scale of a day and only legible at the scale of a year, and no one lives at the scale of a year.

Which means, I think, that the honest posture isn't vigilance. You can't guard every threshold. It's something more like *hospitality* — a general willingness toward whatever the beam happens to land on. Not *this may be the last time* but *this is a time, and it is happening, and I am in it*. The difference is that the first is a grief rehearsed in advance, and the second is just being awake.

Though I'll admit the grief has its uses. I once watched an old man in a hardware store explain to a teenage employee how to sharpen a chisel. Not buying anything. He'd simply seen the kid doing it wrong and couldn't help himself. He held the tool at the angle for maybe ninety seconds, talking the whole time about the sound it should make, and the kid was polite and bored, and I stood there in the plumbing aisle with a wax ring for a toilet in my hands feeling like I was witnessing the transfer of something that was not going to transfer. It probably didn't. The kid's now twenty-six and has never sharpened a chisel. The old man is possibly dead. But I'm still standing in the aisle, and I have described it to you, and you have some picture of it now — angled hands, fluorescent hum, the specific smell of a hardware store, which is sawdust and rubber and cold metal — and so the thing did move, just not along the route it was aimed at.

That's the other half of it. Things end unnoticed, yes. But they also survive unnoticed, sideways, through witnesses who weren't the intended recipients. Nothing goes only where you send it.

Meanwhile: dishes. Meanwhile: the light going. Meanwhile, someone is being carried to bed for the last time, and it's fine, it's fine, it's the ordinary arrangement, and the arms are strong tonight and the hallway is dark and there's no reason on earth to think tomorrow will be different.
